added.note:
Computer vision usually refers to using computers to ingest visual data and doing something with that. For example, we might want to:

- Use our camera footage to track how many visitors are entering our store every day. 
- Analyse an X-ray for signs of cancer.
- Improve the accuracy of Face ID. 

These are all computer vision tasks.
added.title: computer vision

added.note: Agents are LLMs with tools. The objective is to extend the functionalities of a basic LLM. Instead of a simply chatbot, agents are able to perform tasks end-to-end. For example, it could use a web-search tool to find you the cheapest flights to Hawaii and then use a browser tool to book it in your Chrome browser.
added.title: agents

added.note:
Domains are different ways to represent the information within an image. Thinking of images as pixels is pretty intuitive. There are, however, many other ways to represent images too! 

Mathematically, we can think of switching domains as a *change of basis*.
added.title: domains

added.note:
Most agents are reactive. Always-on agents aim to be proactive instead, doing things before you ask for it. For example, it might scan your email and send you a reminder that someone is trying to reach you about your extended car warranty.

Beyond basic scanning capabilities, today’s proactive agents can be incredibly intelligent. I once forgot about a piece of homework. Overnight (without being asked), it scanned my course website and told me I’ve got a deadline today that the instructors added later.

Examples include Meta’s Muse, X’s Grokbot, or ChatGPT dots.
added.title: Always-on Agents

added.note:
Tools are functions that agents can call to get things done. If you asked ChatGPT what’s the weather today, it can’t answer you without external help. The weather today wasn’t in its training data.

It can call a tool to search the internet for the current weather. In practice, Chat might output something like this.

<tool_call>{"name": "web_search", "arguments": {"query": "Berkeley weather"}}</tool_call>

Our ChatGPT app detects “<tool_call>” and immediately knows “hey, the user wants to use a tool now”. It parses the argument and runs a function (usually a simple python one) to search the web for that exact thing. It then returns the answer to Chat, who can now tell you the answer. The exact way these answers are passed around are discussed in harnesses.
added.title: tools

added.note:
The harness can be thought of as the environment that really turns an LLM into an agent. Imagine the following scenario: you want your LLM to write code to create a website. One way it could do this is to output code into your GPT desktop app. You can then paste this code, run it, and preview the app yourself. 

This process, however, is extremely tedious. Harnesses were invented to help automate this. One simple idea is giving an LLM tools and a while loop. *While* website design not good, write or edit code for website, use tool to preview in browser, and determine if satisfactory. Only when you’re satisfied, end the loop.

Harnesses today have grown incredibly complex and often involve many subtle design choices. One area of particular interest is harnesses that recursively improve themselves.
added.title: harness

added.note:
The traditional way in which we represent images in the spatial domain is typically by having three separate *channels* for each pixel. 

Take a standard 1920x1080 image. That would contain approximately 2 million pixels. Each pixel has a certain colour. If I took your mugshot, the center pixels would be skin-colored, and the outer pixels might be the color of the prison facility. We typically represent each pixel as a combination of red, green, and blue, with a scale between 0-255, depending on the intensity. If we say each pixel is represented by a (R, G, B) list, then:

- A pure red pixel: (255, 0, 0)
- A purple pixel: (255, 0, 255)
- A brown pixel: (165, 42, 42)
- A grey pixel: (128, 128, 128)

So really, to represent an image that is 1920x1080, we'd just have about 1080 rows of pixels, with each row containing 1920 of these pixel lists. The total numerical values across all three colors we'd store would then be 1920x1080x3.

Think about how we would represent white pixels or black pixels!
added.title: spatial

added.note:
The frequency domain, in my opinion, is incredibly difficult to really understand, so this explanation will remain overly simplified. The idea is that in most images we've got two areas: high-frequency areas and low-frequency ones.

High-frequency areas have lots of fine, rapidly-changing details, such as a photo of the many blades of waving grass on the ground, or a microscropic view of a cell. Low-frequency areas are smooth. Picture a blue sky or a plain and boring white wall.

Consider a black and white image. Instead of representing each pixel as a number representing how bright that pixel is, we instead represent them as complex numbers. This complex number tells us about a certain pattern and how much it is present. For example, if I took an image of a brick wall, vertical and horizontal edges would be very present (since bricks are rectangular), but diagonal edges probably wouldn't be too present.

Frequency domains are useful for image sharpening and blurring. If I wanted to blur an image, I could just delete all the high frequency parts.
added.title: frequency

umwj20q3a.title: Visual-Language Action Models
umwj20q3a.note:
VLAs take in both:
- natural language instructions e.g. "move banana to the left" 
- visual observations e.g. image of the banana on the table 
and output a sequence of actions for a robot to undertake. For example, they could output a sequence of numbers representing translations and rotations a robot arm must do.

They are essentially fine-tuned VLMs that are able to output sequences of robot actions instead of regular text.

umwj2ojaq.title: Double Descent
umwj2ojaq.note:
Classical modern machine learning describes the "bias vs variance" tradeoff - as model complexity increases, our model tends to perform worse on testing data and better on training data, essentially overfitting. 

Double descent proves this is not true, and that as models become sufficiently large, variance starts to dip again, allowing us to achieve models with low bias and variance.

umwiyr9o9.title: mechanistic interpretability
umwiyr9o9.note: The fascinating study of how neural networks work.

umwizxpma.title: post training
umwizxpma.note: How do you make models even better?

umwj0gssf.title: sparse autoencoders
umwj0gssf.note:
The objective of an SAE is to try and find interpretable features within models. For example, a feature corresponding to deception. In an ideal world we'd find that, and remove it. This has not been that successful.

SAEs have two components: an encoder and a decoder. The basic idea: 
1. Take some intermediate representation (x) from the residual stream
2. The encoder E is literally a large, wide matrix and a bias. We take ReLU(Ex + b). 
3. The decoder D is another matrix that maps the ReLU(Ex + b) back into the x's dimension.
4. Apply loss and train encoder and decoder

Consider this more concrete example:
1. The intermediate representation is a 768x1 vector.
2. The encoder E is a 3072x768 matrix + a bias. ReLU(Ex + b_e) has dimensions 3072 x 1. 
3. We use the decoder D of dimensions 768 x 3072 (also has a bias). output = D ReLU(Ex + b_e) + b_d is another vector of 768x1 dimensions.

SAEs have two types of losses. The reconstruction loss determines how well our output matches our input. To prevent the SAE from learning a dense identity map (trivially reconstructing x), we also use a sparsity loss - forcing many activations within the ReLU(Ex +b) to be zero. The hope is that this allows us to identify interpretable features (columns) within D.

umwlgticb.title: top-p
umwlgticb.note: Top-p (or nucleus sampling) means keeping the top most likely tokens until their cumulative probability is more than or equal to p. Typically 0.8 to 0.95.

umwlgtgm2.title: top-k
umwlgtgm2.note: Keep the most probable k tokens.

umwlgt1md.title: inference parameters
umwlgt1md.note: How do we alter the process of when a model generates a response?

umwlgt6rn.title: temperature
umwlgt6rn.note: A value more than or equal to zero. Lower temperature (0-0.3) makes models deterministic, they output fixed, typically rigid-sounding responses. High temperature (past 1) can make models go crazy. Typically we elect around 0.7.

umwlgy8ux.title: constrained decoding
umwlgy8ux.note:
You ensure the model outputs some kind of structured output. This is useful when you want the model to output a very specific format, e.g. valid JSON only. We do this by masking invalid tokens and setting them to negative infinity.

This guarantees a valid output but not a good one. If your model was going to violate the constraints anyway, the output is probably going to be bad.

umwlh3050.title: cot monitoring
umwlh3050.note: Chain-of-Thought monitoring is essentially reading the model's reasoning and from there understanding its thoughts and intents. We would hope that if the model was cheating on a task, it would expose this through its CoT.

umwlh6v7h.title: prefill
umwlh6v7h.note: Prefill is the act of running the entire prompt through the model just once. The weights of each layer are read from memory once and used for all the prompt tokens. This process is compute-bound.

umwlh6vxc.title: decode
umwlh6vxc.note: Decoding is the process of generating tokens one at a time. The weights of each layer are read again and again for each new token. In each layer the new tokens attend to the keys and values of the previous layers (reading the KV cache). Decode is memory bandwidth bound.

umwlhb019.title: KV cache
umwlhb019.note:
When our LLM is generating a response, the keys and values of previously generated tokens do not change. To avoid continuously recomputing these values, we cache them. This process is memory-bound. 

KV cache grows linearly, potentially causing KV caches to overtake model weights themselves in memory usage for extremely long sequences.

umwlhpunw.title: speculative decoding
umwlhpunw.note:
This is a technique used to drastically speed up inference. Not to be confused with greedy decoding - they can actually be used together. We ask a smaller, faster model to generate k tokens (e.g. generate four tokens) and pass these into our larger model. The larger model treats verifying these as a prefill phase, instead of a decode phase, significantly improving latency. If the four tokens are good, keep them. Else, keep the longest acceptable run (first two tokens could be good, last two bad), generate the next token yourself, and continue speculating.

There is clever math that proves this technique is identical in distribution to having the big model generate the answer itself. 

Almost all models being served today likely use some form of speculative decoding.

umwlgqbx7.title: llm
umwlgqbx7.note:
Large language models are predominantly based on the transformer architecture, introduced by researchers at Google in 2017. They surged in popularity after OpenAI launched ChatGPT in November 2022. The term originally referred to models that processed only text, but it now also covers multimodal models that accept images, audio or video alongside text.

Researchers have also explored alternatives, such as the Mamba architecture and diffusion-based generation. Even so, the autoregressive transformer remains the center of attention.

umwlgqbcv.title: vlm
umwlgqbcv.note: Vision Language Models (VLM) take in both images and text. They are multimodal. The simple idea is to use a Vision Transformer to convert the image into a type of embedding the regular Language Model can accept. This lets images "mix" with text, enabling VLMs to answer questions containing both images and text.

umwljuysy.title: ViT
umwljuysy.note: Vision Transformers apply the transformer architecture towards images. They process images in patches (e.g. a 14x14 square) and typically transform each patch into an embedding. Most VLMs consist of combining an LLM and a ViT together.

umwljzler.title: autoregressive
umwljzler.note: Referring to the act of generating a current value using past values. We often say "LLMs are autoregressive", meaning they generate text one token at a time, based on the prompt given + their previously generated tokens.

umwlk1ho5.title: tokens
umwlk1ho5.note:
Tokens are the fundamental units of data that LLMs process. Tokens are often words, parts of words or punctuation. For example, the word "hello" could be one token. The word "multiplayer" might instead be split into two - "multi" and "player". The full stop at the end of a sentence is often a token too. 

Token consumption generally refers to: how many words is your model taking in and outputting? A rough rule is 1 token = 4 characters. Long conversations or model outputs typically lead to high token consumption and incur high costs.

*In practice, leading spaces (" hello") are often part of a token.

umwljzrh2.title: multimodal
umwljzrh2.note: Multimodal refers to different modalities: image, video, or audio. Non-multimodal models typically refer to models that can only process text.

umwixasws.note:
Machine Learning (in a traditional sense) is not the same as generative AI. Instead of trying to generate code for a website, we are usually trying to make a singular prediction.

For example, given the past 5 years of house purchase data (sale prices, location, number of rooms etc), can we predict how much some house today would sell for?
